content:
I am not a mathematician, but I am fascinated by the fact that LLMs seem increasingly capable of formalising proofs in Lean.

Thus, I conducted what seemed to me a simple experiment: I asked ChatGPT to explore a potentially novel proof of the Pythagorean theorem.

The chatbot was able to produce a manuscript and a Lean formalisation.

I share the concern that AI-generated documents may seem convincing while actually containing serious flaws.

Nevertheless, the Lean file compiles successfully.

For this reason, I would welcome expert feedback on the mathematical validity of the proposed derivation, its assumptions (including any hidden circularity), and its possible originality, or whether a similar approach is already known.

Lean 4 source:
https://github.com/alexodas/pythagorean-isotropy-lean/blob/main/PythagoreanIsotropy.lean

Manuscript and DOI:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23326197

Thank you for your time.

Kind regards,
Alessandro Odasso

Alessandro Odasso said:

For this reason, I would welcome expert feedback on the mathematical validity of the proposed derivation, its assumptions (including any hidden circularity), and its possible originality, or whether a similar approach is already known.

I didnt compile your file or anything, but if it compiles (and you didnt do weird things like add axioms); you are safe from circularites or hidden assumptions etc (it could be that the statement is inaccurate, but that's unlikely).

As you may know, there are many proofs for Pythagoras, see here for a collection of over a 100 of them. So, being no expert about the topic, my guess is that at least similar proofs ought to exist, but maybe it is just best to ask ChatGPT about that.

However if the answer turns out to be "no" (or at least "more" no then yes), you might want to submit this to the Palomar Registry. :)

You can also use Comparator if you want to be a bit more paranoid: Even if #print axioms shows no non-standard axioms, it is theoretically possible that a part of the proof cheats by running metaprograms, for example, and if you don't read the full proof carefully, you might not notice.

Here is the Comparator version* of your proof. You should read the left side, which I stripped of intermediate lemmas and the final proof, keeping only the things necessary to state the main theorem (it might be possible to remove more definitions, I didn't invest a lot of time in minimizing, but the smaller the challenge the better). That's the challenge file: You need to trust/understand that it faithfully states the theorem you want to prove.

When you open the page, Comparator will take a while to check your proof, but then you should get a checkmark in the lower-right corner saying that your proof indeed satisfies the challenge on the left side.

edit: (I think a Palomar submission would also involve Comparator.)

*) I had to redirect the link via my homepage because the Comparator link is too long to fit into this margin.

Thanks all for your feedbacks.

@Paul Reichert
I followed your link, I got what seems a positive response

Exactly. The page is cautious with showing you a green checkmark because Lean can't verify for you that the challenge faithfully represents what you want to prove. The outcome you're seeing means that Lean successfully checked that you solved the challenge from the left side.

When you click "I trust this challenge" (if you do), then the result will no longer look quite as scary red.
I'm not proficient about that specific version of the Pythagorean theorem, so I can't give feedback on whether the statement is correct.
